records.name: Lymph node
records.tldr: Small bean-shaped filters along the lymph vessels where immune cells gather. They are often the first place a cancer spreads, so surgeons check them to see how far the disease has gone.
records.summary: A lymph node is organised immune tissue along lymphatic routes. Nearby nodes can be among the earliest sites of spread for many cancers, but drainage does not establish cancer involvement. Nodal findings can inform staging according to the cancer-specific rules. Sentinel-node biopsy identifies and examines the first draining node or nodes. Removing fewer nodes is generally associated with fewer side effects, but sentinel-node biopsy can also cause lymphoedema. Nodes can support antitumour T-cell priming; antigen arrival alone does not establish that this occurred. Afferent vessels bring lymph into a node and efferent vessels carry it out, and a draining node names a route and not a finding of cancer. Immune material and cells reach a node by different routes: soluble antigen can reach resident dendritic cells through conduits in the node before migrating dendritic cells arrive (Sixt et al., 2005, mouse), while lymphocytes are recruited from the blood through high endothelial venules (Brulois et al., 2020, mouse). Lymph is interstitial fluid collected by lymph capillaries and returned to the venous blood (National Cancer Institute SEER training), so lymph and blood are different fluids and a sample of one does not stand in for the other. A tertiary lymphoid structure is an ectopic lymphoid aggregate that forms in tissue such as a tumour, and it is not a lymph node (Schumacher and Thommen, 2022). Size on imaging is a measurement in millimetres and not a finding of cancer or priming, and a report should say which node was measured, by what method and when (OnCo reporting advice). A node has a cortex, a paracortex and a medulla, and B cells and T cells home to separate areas within them (Willard-Mack, 2006); in the mouse, a venous population in the medulla was predicted to recruit myeloid cells rather than lymphocytes, which videomicroscopy confirmed (Brulois et al., 2020). In gene-targeted mice, loss of the chemokine receptor CCR7 altered the organisation of lymphoid organs and stopped skin dendritic cells reaching draining nodes (Förster et al., 1999). Arrival of material in a node does not show that priming succeeded. Pathological involvement means cancer was identified in examined tissue, which differs from a drainage route, enlargement or an imaging observation, and a negative sampled node does not certify the unsampled nodes (the National Cancer Institute notes that a false-negative biopsy gives a false sense of security about the extent of cancer).

notes: A node's capsule surrounds adjoining cortical, paracortical and medullary regions, with B-cell follicles and T-cell regions. These are adjoining tissue regions rather than sealed rooms. Afferent lymph enters the subcapsular sinus near the outer surface and passes toward medullary sinuses and an efferent vessel at the hilum. Efferent lymph can carry cells as well as fluid onward through lymphatics. Its eventual return to venous blood is downstream, rather than a direct junction to the vein shown beside a node in a simplified drawing.

One simplified route for blood is artery, capillary network, high endothelial venule (HEV), then venous outlet; Brulois and colleagues traced these connections in mouse peripheral nodes. Naive lymphocytes can cross from HEV blood into node tissue. In a diagram, keep that cell movement distinct from blood flow and lymph flow; red cells stay in the blood compartment. Label and enlargement leaders do not show transport or specify a unique crossing mechanism or timing. Nor does one illustrated route map every vessel, dictate every cell's path or demonstrate priming.

Imaging, drainage mapping, sampled-tissue pathology and controlled immune-response experiments answer different questions. Record the node, tissue region, collection method and time. In a fictional earlier-antigen example, arrival before migrating dendritic cells is possible, but uptake, presentation and antigen-dependent activation still need their own measurements. Neither arrival nor node size diagnoses cancer involvement or useful priming.

records.name: Inflammation
records.tldr: Inflammation is a tissue response to infection, injury or tissue stress. It can support repair or contribute to harm; the cause, location and duration matter.
records.summary: Chronic inflammation from infection (hepatitis B and C, H. pylori, HPV), irritation (tobacco, asbestos, acid reflux) or disease (ulcerative colitis) supplies growth factors, free radicals that mutate DNA, and blood-vessel growth, and it is estimated to underlie around a fifth of cancers; 'tumour-promoting inflammation' is a recognised enabling characteristic in the hallmarks of cancer. Inflammation can also contribute to immune responses against tumours, but an 'inflamed' or 'hot' pattern alone does not establish benefit from a checkpoint inhibitor (Chen and Mellman, 2017). Aspirin and other anti-inflammatory drugs reduce colorectal cancer risk, and the inflammatory markers CRP and IL-6 track cachexia and prognosis. Inflammation is not the same as infection: infection and injury are classic triggers, and tissue stress or malfunction can induce a graded response, called para-inflammation, that relies mainly on tissue-resident macrophages (Medzhitov, 2008). Recruited cells can support containment and repair, or persist and add to injury, and increased vessel permeability is not the growth of new vessels. Resolution is a coordinated and active process that restores tissue integrity and function, and is not simply everything switching off (Ortega-Gómez et al., 2013). In experimental cancer systems one DNA-sensing pathway has had opposite roles: host STING-dependent sensing was needed for spontaneous CD8 T-cell priming against mouse tumours (Woo et al., 2014), while a tumour-cell response to cytosolic DNA in chromosomally unstable tumours promoted metastasis (Bakhoum et al., 2018). These are contextual mechanisms and not a head-to-head clinical comparison. Inflammation after an intervention does not show tumour-specific immune learning: a local reaction, immunogenic cell death, recognition of untreated cancer cells and clinical benefit each need their own evidence, and one raised blood marker does not identify the source of inflammation. Acute against chronic and local against systemic are separate axes, and they need not share a trigger or a consequence.

notes: Sterile inflammation means an inflammatory response without an initiating infection; tissue injury can provide such a context. A short response is not guaranteed to heal, and persistent signalling does not establish one inevitable outcome. Acute versus chronic describes time, while local versus systemic describes distribution.

Locate tissue signals, the blood-vessel lumen and recruited cells separately. A cell crossing the vessel wall and fluid or proteins entering tissue are different movements, neither a new vessel growing. Swelling, a cytokine concentration, a fraction of marker-positive cells and a mixed-tissue RNA programme also have different units and denominators. State the specimen, time and quantity; a bulk programme does not identify every producing cell. In the fictional swelling-plus-RNA example, no antigen-specific response or target-cell killing was tested. That observation alone identifies neither the cause nor useful tumour immunity.

records.name: Macrophage states beyond M1 and M2
records.tldr: What a macrophage is doing depends on where it came from, where it sits, and the signals and history it has had, so the two-box labels M1 and M2 describe a laboratory comparison and not every macrophage in a tissue. In a tumour, a macrophage's label does not on its own show what it is doing to the cancer or to T cells.
records.summary: A macrophage's lineage is its developmental origin; its state is a set of activity programmes at one time. A state label describes selected features and is not a complete biography. The M1 and M2 scheme grew from simplified experiments, with interferon gamma and microbial stimulation giving M1-like cells and interleukin-4 giving M2-like cells, and it is ambiguous unless the source, the stimulus and the markers are stated. A consensus framework asks authors to report the source of the macrophages, the activators used and a defined set of markers (Murray et al., 2014). When human macrophages were stimulated with diverse signals, 299 transcriptomes revealed a spectrum of activation states that extends the M1 and M2 model (Xue et al., 2014). In mice, tissue-resident macrophages had distinct enhancer landscapes beyond what developmental origin explained, and the local environment could reshape transplanted precursors and even reprogramme differentiated macrophages moved to a new environment (Lavin et al., 2014). Together these support diversity and plasticity without showing that any macrophage can be converted to any desired state.

notes: In a tumour, a tumour-associated macrophage is named for its location, and its state and tested functions are separate questions. A tumour can hold several programmes in different neighbourhoods or at different times. An expression cluster can suggest a repair, interferon or lipid-handling programme, which is a hypothesis; it does not establish that the cells suppress T cells, kill cancer cells or would respond to a macrophage-directed drug. One marker such as CD163 does not establish a universal suppressive state, a change in proportions between two biopsies does not show that the same cells changed state, and the plain statement that M1 is good and M2 is bad loses the tissue and experiment that give a response its meaning.

Macrophages are described with protein panels, flow cytometry and single-cell RNA, and the report needs the identification rules, tissue or culture source, stimulation, collection time and denominator, because a fraction of recovered macrophages is not cells per area of tissue. A function such as engulfment or the effect on stimulated T-cell proliferation needs its own test with viability and comparator controls.

Consider a fictional culture comparison at 24 hours, scored with one method on a 0 to 1 scale of arbitrary RNA programme units. Profile A has interferon, lipid-handling and antigen-display scores of 0.80, 0.35 and 0.65; profile B has 0.45, 0.85 and 0.55. These six invented values are not measurements from Xue et al., fractions of cells or universal M1/M2 cutoffs. Several selected programmes coexist in each profile. The axes are summaries of expression, not independent switches that can be set or reversed at will. Even an antigen-display RNA score needs a separate functional presentation test. A real comparison also needs the macrophage identification rules, source, exposures, sampling time and scoring method. A change in profile proportions between samples would not establish that the same cells converted from one state to another.

records.name: Peripheral tolerance
records.tldr: Peripheral tolerance is the set of controls that restrain mature immune cells after they have developed, which helps stop them reacting against the body's own tissues. Tumours can use the same controls to avoid attack, and a treatment that releases them can also harm healthy organs.
records.summary: Central tolerance acts during lymphocyte development, in T-cell selection in the thymus and B-cell development in bone marrow. Peripheral tolerance acts on mature cells in tissues and lymphoid organs. The two names say when and where restraint operates, not that they are two complete filters that remove every self-reactive receptor. For T cells, tolerance mechanisms that operate in the thymus before the cells mature and circulate are called central tolerance, but not every self-antigen is made in the thymus, so central tolerance alone is insufficient and additional mechanisms restrain mature circulating T cells (Xing and Hogquist, 2012). For B cells, tolerance regulated at the immature B-cell stage in the bone marrow is called central tolerance and works through clonal deletion and receptor editing, while mechanisms that act after B cells leave the bone marrow were described as not fail-safe and mostly reversible (Nemazee, 2017). Several mechanisms contribute: anergy (reduced responsiveness), deletion (removal by cell death), suppression by regulatory T cells, inhibitory pathways and limited supporting signals. Deletion and restraint differ, because a deleted clone is gone and a restrained clone may remain and respond differently under defined conditions. In transgenic mice, cross-presentation of a self-antigen led to deletion of autoreactive CD8 T cells, and adding CD4 helper cells impaired that deletion and caused diabetes in 68 per cent of mice, whereas the CD8 cells alone did not (Kurts et al., 1997). In mice, transferring CD4 cells depleted of CD25-positive cells into athymic recipients caused multiple autoimmune diseases, and giving back CD4-positive CD25-positive cells within a limited period prevented them in a dose-dependent way (Sakaguchi et al., 1995). A separate mechanism acts on ligand supply: CTLA-4 captured CD80 and CD86 from opposing cells by trans-endocytosis, impairing costimulation through CD28 (Qureshi et al., 2011).

notes: A quiet response has other explanations. Immune ignorance is a setting where the relevant cells have not effectively met the antigen, which is different from tolerance after an encounter, and an antibody concentration alone cannot show that self-reactive B cells were deleted or restrained. In a mouse model with a self antigen in the pancreatic islets, a low antigen concentration left CD8 T cells ignorant of it, while a higher concentration allowed cross-presentation and peripheral deletion (Kurts et al., 1999). Tolerance is inferred from mechanism-specific experiments and not from a blood score: a controlled response to a defined antigen, lineage and count evidence for deletion, and coculture or pathway tests for suppression, with cell type, prior exposure and comparator stated. A non-response can also reflect absent receptors, poor viability or an unsuitable assay.

For cancer, many tumour-associated targets are also found in healthy tissue, and normal tolerance helps explain why recognition and activation are not interchangeable. Tumours can exploit regulatory pathways, but a treatment that releases a restraint can also harm normal organs. A neoantigen may differ from the normal molecule, yet a sequence difference alone does not show that it is recognised, that useful activation follows or that it is safe; candidate specificity, natural display and cross-reactivity with healthy tissue are separate tests. A self-similarity calculation screens candidates and does not measure central or peripheral tolerance in a person. Reviews of human tumour antigens note that differentiation antigens are expressed by some tumours and the matching healthy tissue, that responses to melanoma differentiation antigens occur in patients and healthy donors (suggesting central tolerance to them is incomplete), and that the autoimmune side effects of checkpoint blockade likely reflect breakage of peripheral tolerance to antigens of normal tissues (Vigneron, 2015).

records.name: CD163
records.tldr: CD163 is a receptor found on monocytes and macrophages. Detecting it alone does not establish a tumour-supporting function or benefit from a particular drug.
records.summary: CD163 is a receptor expressed by monocytes and mature macrophages. It helps clear haemoglobin-haptoglobin complexes. UniProt also describes a soluble form shed from the cell surface that may be used to monitor macrophage activation in inflammatory conditions. In a tumour sample, CD163 staining identifies cells expressing the receptor. The macrophage-activation consensus recommends describing the cells, their activating conditions and a collection of markers, rather than reducing activation to two fixed M1 and M2 types. The reading rule is to interpret CD163 with the other markers, tissue location and assay conditions; one marker alone does not establish tumour-supporting function or predict benefit from a drug aimed at the macrophage compartment.
